**_Hardware – downgrading_**** _DELL_**** _/_****_HPE_**** _/_****_NTAP_****
_to EW:_** Tim Long is downgrading DELL, HPE, NTAP to EW as he is taking a
more cautious approach on the stocks in his coverage that are more aligned
with Enterprise spending. Valuations have run, commodity costs have helped
revenues, and don't see a meaningful AI inflection yet
([link](https://barclays.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14198989&ad=5001216180&h=1D5UEYq&sig=CIMnrm26KYwrDR4EUz9tzWW5YDM&v=2&url=https://live.barcap.com/go/publications/link?contentPubID%3DFC6aceea0d6a499b0f14c093c6)).
_From the note:_  

  * We entered the year positive on several stocks with Enterprise exposure (DELL, HPE, NTAP) with a more cautious view on some others (CSCO, FFIV, P, HPQ) in the sector. At the time we thought investor concerns around increased memory costs were overdone, and ultimately the Hardware companies proved that they could pass through commodity costs. We are lowering our ratings to Equal Weight from Overweight on DELL, HPE and NTAP, remain Equal Weight on CSCO, FFIV and P, and Underweight on HPQ. 



  * **DELL**. DELL is different than most on this list as it is fairly aligned with the AI trade. Regardless, we believe the way that DELL has executed on offsetting memory inflation is responsible for a big part of the stock performance this year (up ~355%+ YTD vs. SP500 up ~14%).
    * DELL has executed flawlessly across enterprise categories. Guidance calls for just over 100% revenue growth in enterprise servers, mid teens in storage, and mid teens in CSG for FY27. We believe the vast majority of this growth comes from higher ASPs to offset memory inflation (see Figure 4 above). As a result, we expect a meaningful deceleration in growth over the next two years and memory price normalize and potentially decline.  
  * **HPE****.  **HPE is also more than a pure enterprise play given the acquisition of JNPR and increased reliance on networking (about half of operating profits). The stock has also had a good run (up ~186% YTD vs. SP500 up ~14%). 
    * In server and storage, HPE has followed along with industry participants and used higher ASPs to bolster revenues while maintaining GM.  We see less upside as memory prices normalize. 
  * **NTAP**.  We have liked NTAP based on valuation and an under appreciated cloud business (10% of sales, SaaS model, growing ~20% with 85%+ GM).
    * While we are seeing some upside to the storage industry in 2H26 based on NAND pricing, we also expect a normalization next year. 



**_Internet – E-commerce preview -_****_Agents at the Gate:_** Ross Sandler is
out previewing the e-commerce space and between Muse's launch and Instinct's
commentary around $1300/mo of payer GMV (half of which is likely e-commerce),
the debate around persistent agent disintermediation risk in e-commerce has
reignited. Stocks are increasingly trading on that rather than fundamentals,
which seem fine. _From the note:_

  * **The Key Take-Away:** We expect 3Q results to be broadly solid across e-commerce, but the group has come under pressure as investors start to price in the idea that a broad swath of consumer agents may be seeing adoption in '27 (see [_The Battle for the Persistent Consumer AI Agent Begins_(open in new tab)](https://barclays.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14198989&ad=5001216180&h=tGukr0m&sig=8UWQIqVfVerTEoNxHxhjv6j3K9S&v=2&url=https://live.barcap.com/go/publications/link?contentPubID%3DFC6abc6fd4c4ea2f34641bf3bc)). Stripe Link has seen transaction volume soar [38x (open in new tab)](https://barclays.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14198989&ad=5001216180&h=pIoXl8i&sig=XDEo086ogSGvtzXtK5PgqXlYsEG&v=2&url=https://stripe.com/blog/helping-personal-agents-shop-more-intelligently-and-reliably-with-link)month/month on the back of Muse and Instinct shows some early evidence of e-commerce product market fit for persistent agents. It's fairly well understood that agents can disrupt an e-commerce company's advertising take rate over time, but what is less clear is how these products potentially break down the anti-discounting policies employed by scaled players over the years, and lead to market share shifting towards supplier-direct GMV. To the degree that hundreds of millions of users start shopping with products like Muse or Instinct that will tirelessly hunt for the lowest prices, we think merchants likely respond with better (ie - lower) supplier-direct pricing vs. what is often found on marketplaces where fees are prevalent.

**_Internet – Digital Advertising Preview_****:** Ross Sandler is out
previewing the digital advertising space and sees a few new items investors
should consider as we head into ’27. Google may be forced to syndicate search
text ads to competitors shortly, something that could move market share and
unit economics a bit
([link](https://barclays.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14198989&ad=5001216180&h=k1IUf1x&sig=Q2BQIhxl78Jvc9jbpH9zVJCUyVs&v=2&url=https://live.barcap.com/go/publications/link?contentPubID%3DFC6aced89f3b53522487d19a73)).
_From the note:_

  * **The Key Take-Away:** Digital ad stocks are likely to continue to trade on the likelihood or not of AI being a major headwind or tailwind to their business, making current trends far less important than prior quarters (vs. during periods where the market isn’t contemplating major technology shifts). Looking ahead into ’27, key themes are likely to be: 1) impact of persistent consumer AI agents on budget allocation (Stripe Link agentic transactions are up [38x(open in new tab)](https://barclays.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14198989&ad=5001216180&h=pIoXl8i&sig=XDEo086ogSGvtzXtK5PgqXlYsEG&v=2&url=https://stripe.com/blog/helping-personal-agents-shop-more-intelligently-and-reliably-with-link) m/m in Sept), 2) ad progress from new AI native entrants like ChatGPT, and related 3) text ads syndication from Google to competitors. Against this backdrop we remain constructive on META and GOOGL here. Below we recap how search text ad syndication works, and note that every 10% of US market share on a “net” basis that goes to competitors like OpenAI, META or others, would be a ~$12B hit to GOOGL operating income all else equal.

**_2H26 CIO Survey:_** Barclays Research is out with their latest CIO survey
and spend expectations were at 3.9% for 2026 (a slight uptick from prior 2026
expectations of 3.8% collected in our 1H26 survey). Initial 2027 spend
expectations at 4.0%
([link](https://barclays.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14198989&ad=5001216180&h=DRATKKo&sig=IKLhBeSEO1Rp3MCeqexSj38nolg&v=2&url=https://live.barcap.com/go/publications/link?contentPubID%3DFC6aceca393b53522487d19a46)).

  * **CIO expectations for 2026 and 2027.**  Growth expectations for 2026 in this survey ticked up to 3.9% from the prior 3.8% collected in the 1H26 survey. The initial expectations for 2027 calls for slightly better growth at 4.0%. Given the continued memory market dynamics and overall macro uncertainty, we are encouraged that spending expectations remain solid. Looking at regions, both North America and EMEA are seeing increasing spend expectations with NA moving to 4.3% (vs 4.0% in the 1H survey) and EMEA to 3.9% (from 3.1%). Enterprises with IT budgets >$1B and within the $100M-$500M range should drive more of the uptick, with enterprises with IT budgets <$100M expecting lower growth in 2026 than what they had expected in the 1H26 survey. Notably, large enterprises (IT budgets >$1B) expect 3.9% growth, a jump of ~110bps from the 1H survey where they expected ~2.8% growth. 



  * Retail, Restaurants, Healthcare/Biotech,  Manufacturing/Automotive/Construction/Engineering, and TMT industries are expecting the most spend acceleration in 2026. Based on the survey results we collected on AI-related IT spending since introducing the question in 2024, we observed a positive correlation between % of AI-related spend and total IT spend (in the 1H24 survey, AI-related spend as a % of total spend is 3.4% and total IT spend was 3.1%; in 1H25 survey, both increased, to 3.8% and 3.3%, respectively; in 1H26 survey, both has gone up again, to 4.8% and 3.8%; and in the current 2H26 survey, both moved up again, to 5.2% and 4.0%, respectively). Overall, we view 5% of total spend on AI as underwhelming for enterprises. 

** **

  * **Software takeaways.**  The 2H26 survey showed an encouraging backdrop for software spending with IT budget growth expectations slightly growing again vs. 1H26. Growth expectations slightly improved for both public cloud and software apps. We continue to believe enterprises increasingly prioritize AI and cloud investments. Interestingly, cloud spending became more concentrated into #1 cloud providers, with a decline in spending on secondary and tertiary cloud. Microsoft continued to perform well this half, with Azure maintaining its top rank among cloud providers. Within software apps, ERP, BI/Analytics and ITSM remained the top spending priorities, whereas CRM spending expectations continued to decline and now is well below the 2H25 levels. More broadly, the survey continued to indicate a preference for infrastructure and data-oriented spending. On AI models, adoption remained concentrated in several large vendors, with OpenAI taking the lead, and Anthropic and Google both showed some improvement since 1H26. In general, we see results as most favorable for **Microsoft** as the top cloud provider and one of the top data management platform providers, and for **Datadog** in the observability field, although a slight negative for front office focused names including Salesforce, HubSpot and monday.com.

** **

  * **IT Hardware takeaways.** The overall outlook for 2027 shows an upward trend compared to this and last survey's 2026 expectations. Storage and Communications continue to be the strongest verticals, although Storage expectations ticked down compared to last survey with Printing exhibiting downticks too. Repatriation of workloads back from public cloud expectations keep growing, although overall public cloud spending remains dominant (67% spending expectations vs. 63% from last survey). We have gotten more cautious on the enterprise space with our downgrades of **HP Enterprise** , **Dell**  and **NetApp**  following the strong stock performance YTD (See our downgrade note: [Downgrading Some Enterprise Names after a Significant Run and on Enterprise AI Timing(open in new tab)](https://barclays.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14198989&ad=5001216180&h=1D5UEYq&sig=CIMnrm26KYwrDR4EUz9tzWW5YDM&v=2&url=https://live.barcap.com/go/publications/link?contentPubID%3DFC6aceea0d6a499b0f14c093c6)).

**_Hardware - AUSA Conference Takeaways:_** Tim Long with takeaways from the
Association of the United States Army Conference for MSI and AXON
([link](https://barclays.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14198989&ad=5001216180&h=w7cq46W&sig=DLTsyWSamBNH6p7pggySveux7ba&v=2&url=https://live.barcap.com/go/publications/link?contentPubID%3DFC6aceaab2b2b41e7d7ee096b2)).
_From the note:_

  * We recently attended the Association of the United States Army Conference in Washington, DC. AUSA serves as one of the larger trade shows for the defense technology space. MSI and AXON have traditionally been mostly exposed to state and local governments, but each is increasing its activity with federal governments, the military and defense budgets. Each company is now seeing drone-related revenues at about 10% of total sales. over time, we believe MSI and AXON will get higher multiples for being drone plays.

subject: Chris Wood - High Rates vs AI Trade ?
body:
I sat down with Chris Wood in London during his investor meetings.
Unsurprisingly, high interest rates and the AI boom dominated our
conversation.

  

The AI boom is real.**The AI economics are not.**  

The market remains obsessed with AI revenues years into the future, while
ignoring the more immediate question: who is paying for nearly US$1 trillion
of hyperscaler capex?

AI demand is exploding, but token prices are collapsing and monetisation
remains elusive. The real story is that AI is increasingly being funded by
credit rather than cash flow. Chris' question is simple: what happens when the
credit card gets declined?

Until that question becomes impossible to ignore: **own the picks-and-shovels,
gold, energy and financials.**

**  
**

Against a backdrop of rising geopolitical risk, widening fiscal deficits and
structurally higher yields, our preferred portfolio remains surprisingly old-
fashioned!  

  

**_Gold. Energy. Banks. Semiconductor scarcity. Hard assets and visible cash
flows.  _**

**_  
_**

Hard to disagree with Cris on**China**. He remains constructive on **the
market** , but not because of a consumer / macro recovery. Instead he likes AI
infrastructure, cloud, commodities, power equipment and memory. **Alibaba**
and **Tencent** are being punished for AI spending that would be applauded in
the US. That disconnect could become an opportunity if monetisation finally
arrives.

India remains a structural winner through credit growth, electrification and
manufacturing. Korea and Taiwan remain essential AI exposures, but Chris
believes the easy money has already been made. The next big question is not AI
demand, but how long AI financing remains unconstrained.

**Korea and Taiwan: Still invested, but easy money largely made**

Chris remains positive on semiconductors but notes that TSMC, Samsung and SK
Hynix now account for over 30% of MSCI EM, making semiconductor exposure a
major portfolio decision. Earnings remain supported while AI capex continues,
but the key question becomes: when does financing become constrained? He
suggests Korean mid-caps could eventually become beneficiaries if domestic
wealth effects drive new fund inflows

Here are the full sales notes from the meetings I attended with Chris.

  

* * *

  

I sat with **Chris Wood** in some of his London meetings. The conversations
moved from geopolitics and gold to AI financing, US fiscal dominance and the
increasingly differentiated opportunity set across emerging markets.



**_Geopolitics:_**



Chris remains **cautious on geopolitics**. In the Middle East, he sees a
**failure to reach an agreement before the US mid-terms heightening the risk
of renewed escalation** thereafter, with Trump likely to become less
restrained if the midterms don’t go his way (although he does not expect US
boots on the ground). He also believes **Russia may become more aggressive in
Ukraine** , with Putin’s comments on
[_Kaliningrad_](https://jefferies.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14152653&ad=4970558433&h=UYq3iFb&sig=7zAYsdP4sjoawZVKCPyz0fiJVS0&v=2&url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/putin-
warns-west-escalation-kaliningrad-9.7365845) largely going under the radar.



The portfolio conclusion is to **retain energy exposure** ,**** although
**gold remains his highest-conviction trade** , supported not only by conflict
risk but also by deteriorating fiscal positions and reserve diversification by
central banks.



![](cid:image001.png@01DD5634.069418C0)
![](cid:image002.png@01DD5634.069418C0)
![](cid:image003.png@01DD5634.3CBF21B0)



Central banks bought a net **848 tonnes of gold in 2025** and another **345
tonnes in 1H26** , while gold is estimated to represent **25.8% of global
official reserves** , ahead of the euro and second only to the dollar. His
**long-term target remains $6,600/oz**.



**_AI:_**

** **

The liveliest debate was AI. Chris’s base case is that the industry will
**struggle to monetise the scale of capex** now embedded in expectations. His
toll-booth analogy is useful: LLMs may process enormous traffic, but users can
move between them increasingly easily and the toll keeps falling. The **usage-
weighted token-price index is down 55%** from its late-May peak, while the
leading Chinese models processed 76.1tn tokens on OpenRouter in the week to 27
September versus 14.2tn for the leading US models. That is not evidence that
AI demand is weak, but it is evidence that rapidly rising usage does not
automatically create attractive economics for the model owner.



![](cid:image004.png@01DD5635.0B2B1090)



The **funding question is also becoming harder to ignore**. Capex by
Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta rose to **US$376bn in 2025** and is
forecast to reach **US$723bn in 2026** and **US$993bn in 2027**(though some
numbers are way ahead of this). On those numbers, **capex rises from 23% of
revenue in 2025 to 38% in 2026 and 45% in 2027, while absorbing 100% of
operating cash flow this year and 106% next year**. The five hyperscalers,
including Oracle, have already **issued US$229bn of bonds** this year, more
than **double the US$108bn issued in 2025**. AI investment is therefore moving
from cash towards credit. As such, high-yield spreads should be paid close
attention to, but the more difficult risk sits in opaque private-credit
structures. Credit bubble?



![](cid:image005.png@01DD5635.0B2B1090)**![](cid:image006.png@01DD5635.0B2B1090)**





Another interesting thought is the apparent bipolar treatment of AI capex. US
platforms are often rewarded for spending, whereas Chinese internet names seem
to be punished for the same behaviour. Meta’s rerating following Muse shows
how quickly the market will reward evidence that spending is producing a
differentiated product. Chris nevertheless prefers picks and shovels in the AI
trade because current infrastructure demand is visible while the ultimate
economics of the model layer are not. There is also a second-order software
risk if cheaper models and more capable agents compress the value of parts of
the application layer.



I have also attached my summary of our global AI call with Balyne Curtis,
Janardan Menon, and Edison Lee, as well as Conor O’Mara’s recent piece on key
AI ideas and themes.



**_US:_**

**_ _**

Beyond AI, Chris believes the **US share of global equities has peaked**.
America reached a **record 67.2% of the MSCI AC World Index in December 2024
and now represents 64.5%,** while emerging markets trade on 9.7x forward
earnings versus 19.5x for the US. Importantly, this is not a call for an
imminent collapse in US equities, but a mere caution.



![](cid:image007.png@01DD5637.62B6F390)



The fiscal problem sits at the centre of that argument. Net **interest and
entitlements consumed 95.7% of US federal receipts** in the 12 months to
August, with little political appetite to cut Social Security, Medicare or
other benefits. Chris therefore thinks some form of yield fixing may
ultimately become necessary, drawing an analogy with Japan’s experience from
2016 to 2024. This is simply a hypothesis, but I recommend paying closer
attention to the MOVE index versus VIX. If this does occur, however, EM will
likely come back into favour.



Furthermore, Treasury issuance is already heavily concentrated at the front
end: **annualised gross T-bill issuance reached US$27.7tn in the 12 months to
August and represented 84.5% of gross marketable issuance** (Bessent has been
borrowing at the short end and buying at the long end). As a result, Warsh and
Bessent increasingly appear to be pulling in opposite directions. Warsh wants
to shrink the Fed’s balance sheet and withdraw the excess liquidity created by
what he regards as premature easing in 2024, while Bessent appears more
focused on using the Treasury’s balance sheet and issuance strategy to contain
longer-term borrowing costs. The results have so far been unconvincing, with
**yields around 50bps higher than when Treasury buybacks began**. If the
Republicans suffer a heavy defeat in the mid-terms (base case), Warsh could
actually gain greater operational independence to pursue a more hawkish policy
stance. Just some food for thought.



**![](cid:image008.png@01DD5638.7FCCABE0)![](cid:image009.png@01DD5638.7FCCABE0)**



**_Europe:_**

**_ _**

Europe’s structural challenge remains energy. German natural-gas prices are up
142% in dollar terms this year while US gas prices are down 18%, taking the
**German-to-US price ratio from 2.8x at the end of 2025 to 8.2x**. That is a
material competitive disadvantage for energy-intensive industry and helps
explain Europe’s underperformance since the Iran conflict began. Furthermore,
Chris sees **G7 bonds now being in a structural bear market** post 40-year
bull market.



![](cid:image010.png@01DD5639.0B62ECA0)![](cid:image012.png@01DD563A.3257A700)**![](cid:image011.png@01DD5639.0B62ECA0)**



**_Emerging Markets:_**



China is difficult to reduce to one macro label. Household lending was down
1.6% year-on-year in August and household consumption remains only 40% of
nominal GDP. Xi, however, does not appear inclined to deliver the type of
broad stimulus markets repeatedly expect, absent a more serious threat to
social stability, and households still prefer deposits to equities. Mutual-
fund flows are therefore a useful indicator of whether that behaviour is
changing.



**![](cid:image013.png@01DD563A.3257A700)**



Positioning adds another layer. We are seeing Alibaba and Tencent used as
funding longs, with China internet being punished for AI capex that would
often be rewarded in the US. That creates an opportunity if spending begins to
produce visible cloud or model monetisation, but it also means the market
needs proof rather than another capex promise. Alibaba is particularly
interesting as a broader AI derivative through its dominant Chinese cloud
position and T-Head chip exposure. Chris remains overweight China, but his
portfolio combines platforms with oil, metals, power equipment, semiconductor
equipment and memory rather than relying on a simple consumption recovery.



Hong Kong is cleaner than China. Chris would look to add on a Fed-induced
pullback, although if the US is only at the start of a tightening cycle the
entry point may still be ahead of us.



India remains one of Chris’s preferred markets. Gross fixed-capital formation
is running at 32.4% of GDP, while **bank credit growth accelerated to 18.1%
year-on-year** in mid-September and deposits grew 17.3%. He likes financials
as credit growth recovers, and our Bhaskar, our analyst, sees an attractive
setup in selected NBFCs after a roughly 9% monthly correction. Historical
tightening cycles suggest much of the derating occurs before the first hike,
while prime housing financiers and diversified NBFCs with more floating-rate
assets can benefit from margin expansion. Bhaskar’s preferred names are Bajaj
Finance, Aditya Birla Capital, Cholamandalam Investment and Shriram Finance.



**![](cid:image014.png@01DD563A.3257A700)**



The broader India story remains one of renewables, electrification and
manufacturing build-out (following China’s blueprint). **Hitachi Energy India
remains a preferred name** despite its demanding valuation. It is also
interesting to note that Indian mid-caps have outperformed large caps, though
the Nifty MidCap now trades at 22.6x forward earnings versus 16.9x for the
Nifty. Further, the semiconductor trade will need to cool before global
attention and capital rotate decisively back towards India, while the rupee
has remained a drag for dollar investors (though RBI hikes should provide some
support). Improving India-China relations are another potential upside, as a
further opening of trade would benefit industrial supply chains in both
countries.



**![](cid:image015.png@01DD563A.C3593C00)![](cid:image016.png@01DD563A.C3593C00)**



Korea and Taiwan are now too large for emerging-market investors to ignore.
**TSMC, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix represent 30.5% of MSCI EM, up from
10% at the start of 2023** , so simply being equal-weight semiconductors is
itself a substantial decision. Chris remains invested but believes the easy
money has been made. As long as hyperscaler capex continues to be financed,
the earnings remain supported. **But when will the credit card be switched
off?** Korean mid-caps may be the next beneficiaries if the wealth effect from
large-cap performance translates into domestic mutual-fund inflows, but we
would have to look closer at the data.



![](cid:image017.png@01DD563A.C3593C00)



Chris is cautious on energy-importing ASEAN markets while the Iran conflict
keeps fuel costs elevated, although Singapore is the exception, while he
recommends adding exposure in Brazil on the prospect of a more pro-business
policy mix (historically whoever has won the first round hasn’t lost the
second).



My main takeaway is that **selectivity** is more important than ever. Chris is
positioning for a world of fiscal and geopolitical deterioration. Own gold and
energy against macro risk; own financials where nominal growth and credit are
accelerating; own the semiconductor and infrastructure businesses where
scarcity supports earnings; and be much less willing to capitalise distant AI
revenues.



Kind regards,

Cristina.
